title: The End of Education Reform, or a New Beginning?
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler looks back on a decade of American education reform built on teacher quality, order, testing and Common Core, and judges that it did not work. She argues the neglected story is what gets taught and how: educators are trained in ideas about reading comprehension and discovery learning that conflict with cognitive science. Comprehension depends on background knowledge rather than generic skills, so time spent on skills like finding the main idea is largely wasted. Test-driven reform made this worse by squeezing science and social studies out of the curriculum, hurting the children who rely on school for knowledge. She points to a growing shift toward knowledge-building literacy curricula while cautioning that such curricula need teacher support and better measures than current standardized tests.
points: Reform of the 2010s failed because it ignored curriculum content and the training teachers receive in how learning works.
Comprehension depends far more on topic knowledge than on transferable skills such as finding the main idea.
Test-score pressure narrowed elementary curricula by crowding out social studies and science, especially in low-scoring schools including charters.
Novices learn more from expert explanation and guided discussion than from discovering knowledge themselves.
Knowledge-building curricula show promise but need teacher support and assessments tied to what students were actually taught.
quotes: None of this worked. To be sure, some poor kids got a better education than they otherwise would have. But American students’ scores on international and national tests are stagnant or declining, and the gap between high- and low-achievers is widening.

Teachers spend hours every week believing they’re teaching comprehension “skills” –think “finding the main idea”—when in fact they’re wasting precious time. As cognitive science has demonstrated, comprehension depends far more on how much you know about the topic than on generally applicable “skill.

But cognitive scientists have found that when learners don’t know much about a topic, it’s far more effective for an expert to explain it and guide discussion than for them to try to figure it out on their own.

Standardized tests seem to measure comprehension skills, so schools have spent more and more time trying to teach them. The result has been the near elimination of social studies and science, especially in elementary and middle schools where scores are low—including charters.
Nor is simply adopting a new kind of curriculum a panacea. Teachers need support to implement it well, and especially to adapt it so that struggling students can reap its benefits.
Maybe we still don’t know exactly “what works” in the classroom. But we do know what science has discovered about how kids learn, and we need to make use of it.
